Nia prepares a timeline for a classroom wall. The chart has room for four word-frequency series. Each series must compare speeches of different lengths fairly.

Raw counts tend to be higher in longer speeches. Rates per thousand alphabetic
tokens provide a comparable scale. However, one short document can still
produce an unusually high rate.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- count selected words by speech year.
- normalize word counts per thousand alphabetic tokens.
- put a mark on rates from very short speeches.
- recompute each peak after removing its peak speech.
- compare one trajectory with a permutation null.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Count words by speech

A **trend** is a pattern over time. Counts alone do not prove a trend. Comparable rates reduce the effect of speech length on the comparison.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(ggplot2)

source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")
source("R/permutation-null.R")

paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()

speeches <- paragraphs |>
  summarise(text = paste(paragraph, collapse = "\n"), .by = c(speech_id, year, president, party))

speech_tokens <- speeches |>
  select(speech_id, year, president, text) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  filter(str_detect(word, "^[a-z]+$"))

speech_lengths <- speech_tokens |>
  count(speech_id, year, president, name = "total_alphabetic_tokens")

target_words <- c("america", "freedom", "constitution", "children")
min_tokens_for_rate <- 500L

length_context <- speech_lengths |>
  summarise(
    median_alphabetic_tokens = median(total_alphabetic_tokens),
    minimum_alphabetic_tokens = min(total_alphabetic_tokens)
  )

trend_counts <- speech_tokens |>
  count(speech_id, year, president, word, name = "count") |>
  filter(word %in% target_words) |>
  right_join(
    expand_grid(speech_lengths, word = target_words),
    by = join_by(speech_id, year, president, word)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    count = coalesce(count, 0L),
    per_thousand_alphabetic = count / total_alphabetic_tokens * 1000,
    below_min_tokens = total_alphabetic_tokens < min_tokens_for_rate,
    word = factor(word, levels = target_words)
  ) |>
  arrange(word, year)

trend_summary <- trend_counts |>
  group_by(word) |>
  arrange(desc(per_thousand_alphabetic), year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  reframe(
    total = sum(count),
    speeches_with_word = sum(count > 0),
    max_rate = round(first(per_thousand_alphabetic), 2),
    max_year = first(year),
    max_count = first(count),
    tokens_at_max = first(total_alphabetic_tokens),
    max_rate_flag = if_else(first(below_min_tokens), "under 500 tokens", "ok"),
    rate_excluding_largest = round(max(per_thousand_alphabetic[-1]), 2),
    year_excluding_largest = year[-1][which.max(per_thousand_alphabetic[-1])],
    guarded_rate_excluding_largest = round(
      max(
        per_thousand_alphabetic[-1][
          total_alphabetic_tokens[-1] >= min_tokens_for_rate
        ]
      ),
      2
    ),
    guarded_year_excluding_largest = year[-1][
      total_alphabetic_tokens[-1] >= min_tokens_for_rate
    ][
      which.max(
        per_thousand_alphabetic[-1][
          total_alphabetic_tokens[-1] >= min_tokens_for_rate
        ]
      )
    ],
    survives_guard = max_rate_flag == "ok" & guarded_rate_excluding_largest >= max_rate * 0.5
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  trend_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Word", "Total count", "Speeches with word",
    "Max per 1,000 alphabetic tokens", "Max year",
    "Count in max year", "Alphabetic tokens at max", "Max-rate flag",
    "Rate excluding largest",
    "Year excluding largest", "Guarded rate excluding largest", "Guarded year", "Survives guard"
  ),
  caption = "Summary of four tracked words across 60 speeches",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The lesson uses four words to illustrate the method. A search across hundreds
of words increases the chance of an unusual-looking series. Reporting only
those series creates a **multiple-comparisons problem**: the search makes chance
patterns easier to find.

A trend analysis must record the number of words examined. It must account for
the number of comparisons or confirm the result on new documents.

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(paragraphs), 1377L),
  identical(nrow(speech_lengths), 60L),
  identical(nrow(trend_counts), 240L),
  identical(as.character(trend_summary$word), target_words),
  identical(trend_summary$total, c(166L, 175L, 207L, 49L)),
  identical(trend_summary$speeches_with_word, c(31L, 36L, 39L, 22L)),
  identical(trend_summary$max_year, c(1993L, 2005L, 1793L, 2001L)),
  identical(trend_summary$max_rate_flag, c("ok", "ok", "under 500 tokens", "ok")),
  identical(trend_summary$survives_guard, c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)),
  identical(as.numeric(length_context$median_alphabetic_tokens), 1958.5)
)
```

The denominator counts lowercase ASCII alphabetic tokens because the tokenizer
removes other tokens before measuring speech length. The table reports each
word's count and highest rate on that scale.

The analysis puts a mark on speeches with fewer than 500 alphabetic tokens. One
occurrence in those speeches contributes at least 2 occurrences per thousand.
The median speech has about 1,959 alphabetic tokens. The cutoff therefore
marks the smallest denominators without excluding most speeches.

## Plot the trajectories

A line chart shows the sequence across the corpus's 236 years. Each dot
is one speech, and each line connects speeches for one word. Open circles mark
rates from speeches under 500 alphabetic tokens.

```{r}
#| label: fig-word-trends
#| fig-cap: "Occurrences per thousand alphabetic tokens for four selected words across 60 inaugural addresses."
#| fig-alt: "Four small line charts, one per word, sharing a vertical scale: america, freedom, constitution, and children. Each panel draws its word in blue over faint grey lines for the other three words. America, freedom, and children reach their highest rates after 1990. Constitution peaks in 1793. Open circles mark rates from speeches under 500 alphabetic tokens."
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"

source("R/lesson-figures.R")

plot_data <- trend_counts |>
  mutate(word = factor(word, levels = target_words))

# Without a `word` column, this copy is drawn in every panel as context.
context_lines <- plot_data |>
  rename(context_word = word)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = per_thousand_alphabetic)) +
  geom_line(
    data = context_lines,
    aes(group = context_word),
    colour = lesson_colours[["context"]],
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = lesson_colours[["accent"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    aes(shape = below_min_tokens),
    colour = lesson_colours[["accent"]],
    fill = lesson_colours[["paper"]],
    size = 1.6,
    stroke = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 21), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(vars(word), ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Three of the four words reach their highest rate after 1990",
    subtitle = str_c(
      "Occurrences per 1,000 alphabetic tokens in 60 inaugural addresses.<br>",
      "Open circles mark speeches under 500 tokens. Grey lines show the other words."
    ),
    x = "Speech year",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_lesson(grid = "y")
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(plot_data), 240L),
  identical(levels(plot_data$word), target_words),
  identical(as.numeric(round(max(plot_data$per_thousand_alphabetic), 2)), 12.35),
  identical(
    as.integer(plot_data$year[which.max(plot_data$per_thousand_alphabetic)]),
    2005L
  ),
  identical(sum(plot_data$below_min_tokens), 8L),
  identical(sum(trend_summary$max_year > 1990), 3L),
  identical(
    as.character(trend_summary$word[trend_summary$max_year < 1990]),
    "constitution"
  )
)
```

The chart shows word rates rather than causes. A rate increase can reflect different word choices, subjects, transcription conventions, speech lengths, or a combination of those factors. Counts alone do not distinguish those explanations.

## Compare the peak with a null model

The largest-contributor check must use the reported statistic. Here that statistic is the peak rate. The analysis recomputes each word's rate after it excludes the speech with the maximum per-thousand value.

A **permutation null** asks what peak appears after the word occurrences are randomly reassigned. The **p-value** is the fraction of those shuffled peaks that are at least as high as the observed peak.

```{r}
constitution_counts <- trend_counts |>
  filter(word == "constitution")

constitution_peak_null <- permutation_null(
  observed = max(constitution_counts$per_thousand_alphabetic),
  replicate_fn = function() {
    assigned_speeches <- sample(
      seq_along(constitution_counts$total_alphabetic_tokens),
      size = sum(constitution_counts$count),
      replace = TRUE,
      prob = constitution_counts$total_alphabetic_tokens
    )
    random_counts <- tabulate(
      assigned_speeches,
      nbins = length(constitution_counts$total_alphabetic_tokens)
    )
    max(random_counts / constitution_counts$total_alphabetic_tokens * 1000)
  },
  replicates = 1000L,
  seed = 5601L,
  alternative = "greater"
)

constitution_peak_null_display <- constitution_peak_null |>
  mutate(across(c(observed, null_mean, null_low, null_high, p_value), \(x) round(x, 3)))

constitution_top_rates <- constitution_counts |>
  arrange(desc(per_thousand_alphabetic), year) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  transmute(
    speech_id,
    year,
    president,
    count,
    total_alphabetic_tokens,
    per_thousand_alphabetic = round(per_thousand_alphabetic, 2),
    denominator_flag = if_else(below_min_tokens, "under 500 tokens", "ok")
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  constitution_top_rates,
  col.names = c(
    "Speech",
    "Year",
    "President",
    "Count",
    "Alphabetic tokens",
    "Per 1,000 alphabetic tokens",
    "Denominator flag"
  ),
  caption = "The highest constitution rates and their denominators",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  constitution_peak_null_display,
  col.names = c("Observed", "Null mean", "Null low", "Null high", "p-value", "Replicates", "Alternative"),
  caption = "Permutation null for the constitution peak rate",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(constitution_top_rates$speech_id[1], "1793-Washington"),
  identical(as.integer(constitution_top_rates$total_alphabetic_tokens[1]), 135L),
  identical(as.numeric(constitution_top_rates$per_thousand_alphabetic[1]), 7.41),
  identical(as.numeric(constitution_peak_null_display$observed), 7.407),
  identical(as.numeric(round(constitution_peak_null$null_mean, 2)), 5.31),
  identical(as.numeric(round(constitution_peak_null$p_value, 3)), 0.233)
)
```

The problem is visible for `constitution`. Its maximum rate is 7.41 per
thousand alphabetic tokens in 1793. That speech has only 135 alphabetic tokens,
so one occurrence creates the peak.

After removal of that speech, the next rate is 6.65 in 1861. The original peak
fails the denominator guard because its document contains fewer than 500
tokens.

Random allocation of the 207 occurrences across fixed speech lengths gives a
null mean of 5.31. The 90% interval is 3.42 to 7.43, with p = 0.233. The
observed 1793 peak is within the range that this allocation can produce.

Trend methods produce a series for the chosen words and dates. The null allocates the same number of word occurrences across speeches in proportion to speech length. It measures the resulting peak without the observed time pattern.

## What to remember

- Normalize word counts per thousand alphabetic tokens before comparing
  speeches.
- Put a mark on rates from very short documents. This lesson uses a 500-token cutoff.
- The four tracked words have different coverage across the 60 speeches.
- The `constitution` peak in 1793 comes from 1 occurrence in a 135-word speech.
- Word-rate change can mix word choice, subject matter, transcription, and length.

Use trend charts to find patterns for closer reading. Compare those patterns after excluding the largest contributor.
